readme_text:
# Jet Set Radio Future — PC recompilation **The original Xbox game, translated into a native Windows program.**
Runs on Windows 10/11, and on the Steam Deck through Proton 11. ![Windows](https://img.shields.io/badge/Windows-10%20%7C%2011-0078D6?logo=windows&logoColor=white) ![Steam Deck](https://img.shields.io/badge/Steam%20Deck-Proton%2011-1A9FFF?logo=steamdeck&logoColor=white) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/game-NTSC%20(US)%20retail%20only-orange) ![Bring your own game](https://img.shields.io/badge/game%20files-not%20included-lightgrey)
This is **not an emulator**. The game's own program is translated, once, into C code on your computer, and that code is compiled into a normal Windows `.exe`. The Xbox's hardware — graphics, sound, controllers, memory card — is recreated by the runtime in `xboxrecomp/`. > [!IMPORTANT] > **You need your own copy of the game.** Nothing from the game is in this > repository: no code, no graphics, no music. The translation is made on your > computer, from your copy. ### How hard is each step? Each section is marked with how much effort it takes: | Badge | Meaning | |---|---| | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen) | Double-click or copy a file. Anyone can do it. | | ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-medium-yellow) | A few more steps, or installing something. Follow the instructions closely. | | ![Hard](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-hard-red) | Typing commands, or system settings. Optional — there is always an easier way. | --- ## Contents | | Section | Difficulty | |---|---|---| | 1 | [What you need](#1-what-you-need) | — | | 2 | [Install the tools (once)](#2-install-the-tools-once) | ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/-medium-yellow) | | 3 | [Get this project](#3-get-this-project) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 4 | [Add your game files](#4-add-your-game-files) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 5 | [Build the game](#5-build-the-game) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 6 | [Play — Option A or Option B](#6-play) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 7 | [Playing on a Steam Deck](#7-playing-on-a-steam-deck) | ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/-medium-yellow) | | 8 | [Controls](#8-controls) | — | | 9 | [Settings (jsrf.ini)](#9-settings-jsrfini) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 10 | [Saves](#10-saves) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 11 | [Updating to a newer version](#11-updating-to-a-newer-version) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 12 | [Troubleshooting](#12-troubleshooting) | — | | 13 | [Reporting a problem](#13-reporting-a-problem) | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) | | 14 | [What's in the folders](#14-whats-in-the-folders) | — | | 15 | [Credits and licences](#15-credits-and-licences) | — | --- ## 1. What you need | | Requirement | |---|---| | 💻 | **A Windows 10 or 11 PC** to build the game. Once built, it also runs on a Steam Deck with **Proton 11** (building on the Deck itself is not supported). | | 💿 | **Your copy of Jet Set Radio Future for the original Xbox — the NTSC (North American) retail release**, as a disc image (`.iso`) or as its files (`default.xbe` plus the folders next to it). | | 💾 | **About 5 GB of free disk space** (mostly Visual Studio). | | 🎮 | **A graphics card with OpenGL 3.3** or newer — practically any GPU from the last ten years. | > [!WARNING] > **Only the NTSC (North American) release works.** The PAL (European) and > NTSC-J (Japanese) releases are built differently inside. The build checks the > game's code and data inside your `default.xbe` and stops if they are not the > right ones. It does **not** compare the whole file: many dumps have a patched > header (region, allowed media), which changes the file's SHA-256 but not the > game, and those work fine. > > To check your copy before building, open a terminal in `jsrf_recomp` and run > `py -3 tools\xbe_info.py` (or `py -3 tools\xbe_info.py path\to\default.xbe`). > It says whether the code matches and, if not, which part differs. --- ## 2. Install the tools (once) ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-medium-yellow)   ⏱️ 15–30 minutes, mostly waiting You need **two free programs**. A third piece, *capstone*, installs itself. Install them in this order. ### Step 1 — Visual Studio 2022 Community (the C compiler) 1. Download it from . 2. Run the installer. When it asks what to install, tick **☑ Desktop development with C++**. Leave the options on the right as they are; they include CMake, which the build also needs. 3. Click **Install** and wait (it is large). > [!TIP] > You never need to open Visual Studio afterwards — the build scripts use it on > their own. ### Step 2 — Python 3 (runs the translator) 1. Download the latest Python 3 from . 2. Run the installer and, **on the first screen, tick ☑ Add python.exe to PATH**, then click **Install Now**. > [!CAUTION] > If you forget to tick **Add python.exe to PATH**, the scripts cannot find > Python. Run the installer again, choose *Modify*, and tick it. ### Step 3 — capstone ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-automatic-brightgreen) Nothing to do: `generate_code.bat` installs it the first time it runs (it needs an internet connection then).
Install it yourself instead (optional) Open **Command Prompt** and type: ``` py -3 -m pip install capstone==5.0.7 ```
--- ## 3. Get this project ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen)   ⏱️ 1 minute Pick one: - **Download the ZIP** — on the GitHub page, click the green **Code** button → **Download ZIP**, then unzip it somewhere with a short path, for example `C:\JSRF\`. - **With git** — `git clone C:\JSRF` You should end up with: ``` C:\JSRF\ ├── xboxrecomp\ the runtime and the translator ├── jsrf_recomp\ the game project — you work in here └── README.md this file ``` > [!NOTE] > Avoid folders that are synced (OneDrive, Dropbox) or have very long paths; > the build creates many files. --- ## 4. Add your game files ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen)   ⏱️ a few minutes Copy **all** of the game's files into `jsrf_recomp\game\` — `default.xbe` and every folder next to it — so that this file exists: ``` C:\JSRF\jsrf_recomp\game\default.xbe ```
💿 I only have a disc image (.iso)   The toolkit can unpack it. Open **Command Prompt** and type: ``` cd C:\JSRF\xboxrecomp py -3 -m tools.xiso unpack "C:\path\to\your\game.iso" -o ..\jsrf_recomp\game ```
--- ## 5. Build the game ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen)   ⏱️ 10–20 minutes the first time Open the `C:\JSRF\jsrf_recomp\` folder in Explorer and double-click, **in order**: | Step | Double-click | What it does | How long | |:---:|---|---|---| | **1** | `generate_code.bat` | Checks your `default.xbe`, then translates the game's program into C code (in `src\recomp\gen\`). | 2–3 min | | **2** | `rebuild.bat` | Compiles everything into `jsrf_recomp.exe`. The first time it also sets up the build folder. | 5–15 min the first time, faster after | Each window ends with ✅ **Done** / **Build OK** when it worked, or ❌ **FAILED — scroll up for the first error** when it didn't (see [Troubleshooting](#12-troubleshooting)). > [!TIP] > You only need `generate_code.bat` again when you update the project > ([section 11](#11-updating-to-a-newer-version)). `rebuild.bat` is what you run > after any change. --- ## 6. Play There are two ways to play. **Pick one.**
🅰️  Option A — Ready-to-play game folder 🅱️  Option B — Straight from the project
![Recommended](https://img.shields.io/badge/-recommended-brightgreen) ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) Double-click **`build_portable.bat`**. It builds the game and copies `jsrf_recomp.exe` and a settings file, `jsrf.ini`, into your game folder (`jsrf_recomp\game\`). From then on, just double-click **`jsrf_recomp.exe` in the game folder**. You can make a desktop shortcut to it, or copy the whole game folder to another PC or a Steam Deck. **Best for:** everyday playing, and the Steam Deck. ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) Double-click **`play_jsrf.bat`** in `jsrf_recomp\`. The game runs from the build folder; its settings are inside the `.bat` file instead of `jsrf.ini`. **Best for:** quick tests after a rebuild, without copying anything.
> [!TIP] > **`F11`** or **`Alt+Enter`** switches between window and full screen at any time.
> To put the game in a different folder with Option A: `build_portable.bat D:\Games\JSRF` --- ## 7. Playing on a Steam Deck ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-medium-yellow)   ⏱️ 10 minutes 1. On your PC, do **[Option A](#6-play)**. Your game folder now holds the game files, `jsrf_recomp.exe` and `jsrf.ini`. 2. Copy that whole folder to the Deck (USB stick, SD card, or over the network), for example to `/home/deck/Games/JSRF`. 3. On the Deck, switch to **Desktop Mode**, open Steam, and choose **Games → Add a Non-Steam Game to My Library… → Browse…**. Set the file type to *All Files*, pick `jsrf_recomp.exe`, and add it. 4. In Steam, right-click the new entry → **Properties → Compatibility** → tick **Force the use of a specific Steam Play compatibility tool** and choose **Proton 11**. 5. Go back to **Gaming Mode** and play. > [!WARNING] > **Tested with Proton 11 only.** Earlier Proton versions have not been tested, > and there are no plans to support them. If something goes wrong on an older > version, switch to Proton 11 first. > [!NOTE] > The provided `jsrf.ini` already has the settings that suit the Deck: > `RECOMP_GL_SCALE=2` (1280×960 inside the game) and `RECOMP_GL_TEX_WATCH=0` > (avoids stutter). ### Choose a power mode Both modes give a steady **60 fps**. They differ in power use and setup. | | 🔋 **Mode 1 — Standard** | 🌿 **Mode 2 — Power saving** | |---|---|---| | **Difficulty** | ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-nothing%20to%20do-brightgreen) | ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/-medium-yellow) | | **Setup** | none | one line in `jsrf.ini` + the PowerTools plugin | | **Power use (measured)** | about 7 W | 3–4 W in quieter areas, 5–7 W in busy ones | | **Battery and heat** | normal for a demanding game | noticeably longer battery, cooler, quieter fan | | **Affects other games** | no | no, when set per game in PowerTools |
💡 Why is there a difference? While the game runs, its threads constantly hand work to each other and wait for the other side to finish. They can wait in two ways: - **Spinning:** the thread keeps checking, over and over, whether the other side is done. It reacts instantly, but a CPU core stays busy the whole time — that is power spent on waiting. - **Sleeping:** the thread tells the system "wake me when it's done" and the core rests. That saves a lot of power, but it has a side effect on the Deck: with its cores resting, the Deck lowers the CPU clock, and its default settings take 2–3 seconds to raise it again when the game suddenly needs it. In busy areas like 99th Street that shows up as a few seconds under 50 fps. Mode 1 keeps the spinning, so the Deck always runs fast. Mode 2 sleeps, and fixes the side effect by telling the Deck to raise its clock straight away (the **performance** CPU governor).
#### 🔋 Mode 1 — Standard ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-nothing%20to%20do-brightgreen) Leave `jsrf.ini` as it is. The line `;RECOMP_SLEEP_WAITS=vblank` stays switched off (it starts with `;`), so the default is used: only one small wait sleeps — the one that avoids music crackling — and the rest spin. #### 🌿 Mode 2 — Power saving ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-medium-yellow)   ⏱️ 15 minutes the first time > [!IMPORTANT] > Do **both** steps. With only Step 1, busy areas drop under 50 fps for a few > seconds whenever the CPU has to speed up. **Step 1 — let the game sleep while it waits** ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/-easy-brightgreen) Open `jsrf.ini` (in the game folder) with a text editor and change this line: ```diff - ;RECOMP_SLEEP_WAITS=vblank + RECOMP_SLEEP_WAITS=all ``` That is: remove the `;` and change `vblank` to `all`. Save the file. **Step 2 — set the CPU governor to "performance" with PowerTools** ![Medium](https://img.shields.io/badge/-medium-yellow) PowerTools is a plugin for **Decky Loader**, a free plugin system for the Deck's Quick Access menu. 1. **Install Decky Loader (once).** Switch to **Desktop Mode**, open a web browser, go to , download the installer and run it (choose the normal *release* version). Then go back to **Gaming Mode**. 2. **Install PowerTools (once).** Press the **`…`** (Quick Access) button. A new **plug icon** (Decky) is now at the bottom of the menu. Open it, then the **store icon** at its top, search for **PowerTools** and install it. 3. **Set the governor for this game.** Start Jet Set Radio Future, then press **`…`** → plug icon → **PowerTools**: - turn on the **per-game** setting, so the change only applies to this game; - in the **CPU** section, set the **governor** to **performance**. If the governor is not shown, turn on the advanced or per-core CPU options first. > [!NOTE] > The labels can differ a little between PowerTools versions — look for > *governor* in the CPU options. PowerTools remembers the setting, applies it > every time you start the game, and puts your normal setting back for other > games.
⌨️ Without PowerTools — by hand in Konsole   In **Desktop Mode**, open **Konsole** and type (it asks for your sudo password — if you have never set one, run `passwd` first): ``` echo performance | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*/scaling_governor ``` ⚠️ **This applies to every game until you restart the Deck.**
--- ## 8. Controls **A controller** (Xbox, PlayStation, the Steam Deck's own) works as an Xbox controller. **The keyboard** works as controller 1: | ⌨️ Keyboard | 🎮 Xbox controller | |---|---| | Arrow keys | D-pad | | Numpad `8` `2` `4` `6` | Left stick | | `I` `K` `J` `L` | Right stick | | `Z` `X` `A` `S` | A / B / X / Y | | `Q` `E` | White / Black | | `1` `3` | Left / Right trigger | | `Enter` | START | | `Backspace` | BACK | > [!NOTE] > The game window must have the focus for keys to count. --- ## 9. Settings (jsrf.ini) ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen) Settings live in `jsrf.ini`, next to `jsrf_recomp.exe`. Open it with Notepad. Each setting is one line, `NAME=value`. A line starting with `;` is switched off — delete the `;` to switch it on. The full list with explanations is in `jsrf_recomp\jsrf.ini.example`. The ones you are most likely to want: | Setting | What it does | |---|---| | `RECOMP_GL_SCALE=2` | Internal resolution: `1` = 640×480 (original), `2` = 1280×960, `3` = 1920×1440, `4` = 2560×1920. Higher is sharper and needs a stronger GPU. | | `RECOMP_FULLSCREEN=1` | Start in full screen. | | `RECOMP_GL_VSYNC=1` | Wait for the screen's refresh (no tearing). | | `RECOMP_APU_GAIN=0.5` | Master volume. | | `RECOMP_APU_REVERB=0` | Turns off the echo effect in some areas. | | `RECOMP_SAVE_DIR=…` | Where the `savegame` folder (the cache and partition images) goes, if not in the game folder. Your save itself stays in `UDATA`. | | `RECOMP_SLEEP_WAITS=…` | Steam Deck power mode — see [section 7](#choose-a-power-mode). | | `RECOMP_QUIET=1` | Leave this on: it turns off diagnostics that cost speed. | > [!CAUTION] > **Do not change** the lines in the `[game]` section of `jsrf.ini` — the game > needs them to start. If you play with **Option B** (`play_jsrf.bat`), its settings are inside the `.bat` file instead (same names). --- ## 10. Saves ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen) Your save is in the **`UDATA`** folder of your game folder (for example `jsrf_recomp\game\UDATA\`), next to `TDATA`, which holds the game's own settings. These two folders are tiny: copy them to back up your progress, or to move it to another PC or the Deck. | Folder in the game folder | What it holds | Size | |---|---|---| | `UDATA\` | 💾 **your save** | tiny | | `TDATA\` | the game's own settings | tiny | | `savegame\` | the Xbox hard-disk cache (`Cache\`) and partition images (`.img`) — rebuilt automatically if deleted | up to ~5 GB | | `shader_cache\` | compiled shaders, so effects don't stutter the second time — rebuilt automatically if deleted | small | > [!TIP] > The `.img` files show a size of up to 2 GB each but are *sparse*: their > **Size on disk** (right-click → Properties) should be about 0. If it is the > full size — files made by an older build — close the game and delete them; > they come back empty and sparse on the next start. When copying the game to a > Steam Deck, leave `savegame\` out: a FAT32/exFAT stick would copy the full > ~5 GB, and the Deck recreates it by itself. > [!NOTE] > Despite its name, `savegame\` does **not** hold your save — only data the game > rebuilds by itself. You can delete it to free space (with the game closed); > the first run after that loads a little slower while the game copies its > files again. --- ## 11. Updating to a newer version ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen)   ⏱️ 5–10 minutes 1. Get the new version of the project (download the ZIP again, or `git pull`). If you download a ZIP, unzip it **into a new folder** and move your `game` folder across — don't copy the old `build` folder. 2. Double-click **`generate_code.bat`**, then **`rebuild.bat`** — or **`build_portable.bat`** if you play with Option A. Your `jsrf.ini` and saves are kept. --- ## 12. Troubleshooting | ❌ You see | ✅ What to do | |---|---| | `Python 3 not found` | Install Python ([section 2](#step-2--python-3-runs-the-translator)) with **Add python.exe to PATH** ticked. Close and reopen the window afterwards. | | `could not install capstone` | Check the internet connection and run `generate_code.bat` again, or run `py -3 -m pip install capstone==5.0.7` in Command Prompt. | | `default.xbe not found` | The game files must be in `jsrf_recomp\game\`, with `default.xbe` directly in it (not in a subfolder). | | `this default.xbe is not the one the analysis was made from` | Your copy is a different version — most likely the PAL (European) or NTSC-J (Japanese) release. Only the NTSC (North American) retail release works. | | `No recompiled code yet in src\recomp\gen` | Run `generate_code.bat` before `rebuild.bat`. | | `cmake` not found, or `Visual Studio 17 2022` not found | Install Visual Studio 2022 with **Desktop development with C++** ([section 2](#2-install-the-tools-once)). | | `MSB1009: Project file does not exist` (`ALL_BUILD.vcxproj`) | An earlier setup failed halfway. Delete the `jsrf_recomp\build` folder and run `rebuild.bat` again (newer versions do this for you); if it fails again, the real error is right after **Configuring...** | | CMake says the cache or source folder doesn't match | You moved or copied the project. Delete the `jsrf_recomp\build` folder and run `rebuild.bat` again. | | `BUILD FAILED` with something else | Scroll up to the first line that says `error`, and report it ([section 13](#13-reporting-a-problem)). | | `Could not copy the exe … is the game still running?` | Close the game and run `build_portable.bat` again. | | The game is slow or stutters | Lower `RECOMP_GL_SCALE`; make sure `RECOMP_QUIET=1` is on; on a laptop, plug it in. | | Problems on the Steam Deck (or under Proton/Linux) with a Proton version other than 11 | Switch to **Proton 11** ([section 7](#7-playing-on-a-steam-deck)). Only Proton 11 is tested; older versions are not supported. | | Busy areas on the Deck drop below 50 fps for a few seconds | You set `RECOMP_SLEEP_WAITS=all` without the performance governor — do both steps of [Mode 2](#-mode-2--power-saving), or go back to Mode 1. | --- ## 13. Reporting a problem ![Easy](https://img.shields.io/badge/difficulty-easy-brightgreen) A log lets someone see what happened. | If you play with… | Do this | |---|---| | 🅰️ **Option A** (exe in the game folder) | In `jsrf.ini`, remove the `;` in front of `RECOMP_LOG=stderr.txt`, and put a `;` in front of `RECOMP_QUIET=1`. Play until the problem happens, close the game, and send `stderr.txt` from the game folder. | | 🅱️ **Option B** (from the project) | Double-click `run_jsrf.bat` instead of `play_jsrf.bat`; it writes `stderr.txt` in `jsrf_recomp\`. | Say what you did, what you expected and what happened instead, and whether it was on a PC or a Steam Deck. > [!TIP] > Put the `;` back in front of `RECOMP_LOG` afterwards — the log makes the game > slower. --- ## 14. What's in the folders **`jsrf_recomp\` — the scripts you use:** | File | Use it to | |---|---| | `generate_code.bat` | translate your `default.xbe` into C (after getting or updating the project) | | `rebuild.bat` | build the game | | `build_portable.bat` | build and put the exe + `jsrf.ini` in the game folder (**Option A**) | | `play_jsrf.bat` | play from the project (**Option B**) | | `run_jsrf.bat` | play with a full log, for reporting a problem | | `debug\` | tools for diagnosing freezes and graphics problems (developers) |
📁 The rest of the folders | Folder | What it is | |---|---| | `jsrf_recomp\game\` | your game files go here (never uploaded) | | `jsrf_recomp\src\` | the project's own code (`main.c`, `recomp_manual.c`) and, after step 5, the generated code in `src\recomp\gen\` (never uploaded) | | `jsrf_recomp\analysis\` | the map of the game's program the translator works from: where each function starts and ends, names, calling conventions — addresses and names, no game code | | `jsrf_recomp\tools\` | the scripts behind the `.bat` files, and developer tools | | `jsrf_recomp\portable\` | the default `jsrf.ini` that `build_portable.bat` copies | | `jsrf_recomp\README_JSRF.md` | the development history of every version, with measurements | | `xboxrecomp\` | the toolkit: the translator (Python) and the runtime that recreates the Xbox (kernel, NV2A graphics on OpenGL, MCPX audio, controllers) |
--- ## 15. Credits and licences - This project's own files (everything outside `xboxrecomp/`) are MIT licensed — see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). - `xboxrecomp/` is MIT licensed (see `xboxrecomp/LICENSE`). Some of its audio files come from [xemu](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu) under LGPL-2.1 — see `xboxrecomp/NOTICE` for the full list and their authors. - *Jet Set Radio Future* is © SEGA. Xbox is a trademark of Microsoft. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by SEGA or Microsoft, and includes none of their code or content.

readme_text:
# Saru Get You: Saru Saru Daisakusen Recompilation

![Saru Get You: Saru Saru Daisakusen](include/image/SaruSaruBigMission.png)

This is a recompilation project of **Saru Get You: Saru Saru Daisakusen**,
with the aim of making the game available on Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android
with improved performance and configurability, and providing a foundation for
translating the game.

**Status: early, not yet verified playable end to end.** On macOS arm64 the
game boots, renders and plays sound in a window through the title screen, the
attract demo, the save menu and the stage hub, with 60 FPS frame interpolation,
an adjustable FOV and a launcher in English and Japanese. Linux arm64 installs
and runs the game; Windows x64 and Linux x64 build in CI but have not yet been
played. See the [project plan](PLAN.md) and the
[profile instructions](profiles/sarusaru/README.md).

Releases contain only the launcher: the first time you press **Play**, it
builds the game on your machine from your own disc. No game files or game code
are distributed. An unofficial English machine translation of the game's text
is an optional download from the launcher's settings, published separately in
[sarusaru-translations](https://github.com/jackgllghr/sarusaru-translations).

## Roadmap

The following milestones describe the project's goals, rather than currently
supported features. See [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) for detailed progress and acceptance criteria.

- Complete faithful gameplay: rendering, audio, movies and PSP services, verified
  through a representative level, saving, restarting and reloading.
- Verify PSP-compatible saves, with safe writes, backups, import and export.
- Improve graphics and controls with adjustable resolution, verified FOV and
  framerate options, fully rebindable controls and analog camera support.
- Build a shared launcher and in-game settings UI for ISO installation,
  configuration and save management, including Android setup and touch support.
- Provide translation infrastructure for text, fonts and texture replacements,
  with translation-pack support and Japanese fallback.
- Deliver tested, reproducible builds for Windows, macOS, Linux and Android,
  once platform verification and release requirements are met.

## PSPRecomp framework

The project is built on PSPRecomp. The upstream framework documentation follows below.

PSPRecomp is a static recompilation framework for PSP software. It reads an Allegrex/MIPS executable, analyzes guest code, emits C++ translation units, and runs them through a native host runtime. An opt-in interpreter supports code outside the compiled corpus; normal gameplay uses the compiled functions.

The [PPSSPP save-state foundations](profiles/sarusaru/docs/ppsspp-save-states.md)
include inspection and repacking tools. Native quick states can be saved from
the launcher's **Saves** screen and its in-game counterpart, with five thumbnail
slots. Select + R1 saves and
Select + L1 loads; keyboard defaults are F5 and F8. PPSSPP gameplay-state
interchange remains unfinished.

The repository is split between the reusable framework and the game-specific
SaruSaru profile (`profiles/sarusaru`).

## Repository layout

```text
include/psprecomp/   Public runtime and Allegrex interfaces
src/                 ELF/PRX loading, decoder, memory, runtime and support code
tools/               Generic analyzer, recompiler and reverse-engineering helpers
tests/               Framework regression tests
configs/             Generic examples and PSP NID data
profiles/            Game-specific hosts, generated code, configuration and tests
  sarusaru/          Saru Get You: Saru Saru Daisakusen profile
```

Game-specific addresses, HLE behavior, native fast paths, renderer integration and generated AOT code belong under a profile. The framework should remain usable without any profile selected.

## Requirements

- CMake 3.20 or newer and Ninja
- A C compiler for the profile's bundled Zstandard codec, and a C++20 compiler
  (Apple clang, GCC 13, Clang 17 or Visual Studio 2022)
- Python 3.10 or newer for the profile's scripts

See the [profile requirements](profiles/sarusaru/README.md#requirements) for
each host's packages.

## Build the framework only

```bash
cmake -S . -B out/framework -DPSPRECOMP_PROFILE=""
cmake --build out/framework --config Release
ctest --test-dir out/framework -C Release --output-on-failure
```

This builds `psprecomp_core`, `psp_analyze`, `psp_recomp`, `dump_function` and the framework tests.

## Build a profile

Profiles are selected with `PSPRECOMP_PROFILE`:

```bash
cmake -S . -B out/sarusaru -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DPSPRECOMP_PROFILE=sarusaru -DSARUSARU_GAME_MODULE=OFF
cmake --build out/sarusaru
```

This builds the launcher and tests without game files. To build and play the
game from your own disc, use the profile's scripts:

```bash
python3 profiles/sarusaru/scripts/build_and_run.py --iso '/path/to/game.iso'
```

## Create another profile

See [`docs/PROFILE_GUIDE.md`](docs/PROFILE_GUIDE.md). A new title normally provides its own generated corpus, HLE/profile host, configuration, tests and optional native fast paths without modifying the framework for game-specific addresses.

## Game files

No commercial game executable or asset is included. PSPRecomp does not ship an EBOOT decryption implementation. Profiles expect files obtained from the user's own copy in the format documented by that profile.

## Source provenance

See [`docs/SOURCE_PROVENANCE.md`](docs/SOURCE_PROVENANCE.md) for the project rules around independently written code, profile boundaries, decryption and third-party source.

## Third-party code

The framework is MIT licensed. Individual profiles may include separately licensed dependencies or assets; their notices stay beside those files. The SaruSaru profile lists its bundled dependencies in `profiles/sarusaru/THIRD_PARTY.md`.

## License

PSPRecomp framework code is distributed under the MIT License. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

## Credits

- [PSPRecomp](https://github.com/jessicanataliagta/PSPRecomp) — the recompilation framework this project builds on.
- [SDL3](https://www.libsdl.org/) — windowing, input and audio output.
- [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/) — music and movie decoding.
- [Vulkan](https://www.vulkan.org/) and [MoltenVK](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/MoltenVK) — rendering.
- [tiny-AES-c](https://github.com/kokke/tiny-AES-c) — the installer and PSP save-data support.
- [Dear ImGui](https://github.com/ocornut/imgui) — the launcher's interface.
- [Luckiest Guy](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Luckiest+Guy) and
  [M PLUS Rounded 1c](https://github.com/coz-m/MPLUS_FONTS) — the launcher's fonts.
- [TeamGDB](https://github.com/TeamGDB) — their Yakumo project served as inspiration.

## Legal disclaimer

This is an unofficial, independent project and is not affiliated with, endorsed
by, or sponsored by Sony Interactive Entertainment.

Saru Get You (サルゲッチュ / Ape Escape), the franchise to which **Saru Get You:
Saru Saru Daisakusen** belongs, is a trademark of **Sony Interactive Entertainment
Inc.** See the [official PlayStation trademark attribution](https://www.playstation.com/ja-jp/games/ape-escape/).
The original game and its artwork remain the property of their respective
rights holders. All other trademarks belong to their respective owners.

Users must supply their own legally obtained copy of the game. The project's
source-code license does not grant any rights to the original game, its assets
or its trademarks.

readme_text:
# Kula World Recompiled

A static recompilation of **Kula World** (PAL, SCES-01000) to native Linux, macOS and Windows (comming soon!), built on [psxrecomp](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/psxrecomp)
and [recomp-ui](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/recomp-ui).

The game's MIPS code is translated to C ahead of time and compiled into a
native executable. No emulator core runs the game. Bring your own disc image;
a retail BIOS is optional because the bundled, MIT-licensed OpenBIOS works.

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Title screen at 16:9](docs/images/title.png) | ![Level select submenu](docs/images/level-select.png) |
| ![World 3 in widescreen, HUD in the corners](docs/images/widescreen-world3.png) | ![World 9 in widescreen](docs/images/widescreen-world9.png) |

## AI-Assisted Development
> [!IMPORTANT]
> This project was created with significant AI assistance, and that is intentional and transparent.
>
> Parts of the codebase were generated with AI, but the application was not shipped as unchecked output. The generated code was reviewed, corrected, and validated by a human developer before being kept in the project.

## Status

Playable; all ten worlds start and run (checked via Level Select, the ending FMV is not verified yet). The recompiled game reaches the same
attract demo, with the same timer values, as the psx-beetle reference
emulator.

| Platform | State |
|---|---|
| Linux (x86-64, tested on Alpine/musl) | builds and runs; tested headless under Xvfb |
| macOS (Apple Silicon, M1 Pro) | builds and runs at 50 fps; audio, memory card, launcher, keyboard verified |
| Windows | not tested |

## Mods

All mods are switchable in the launcher (recomp-ui).

| Mod | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Level Select | on | "Arcade" opens START / WORLD / LEVEL. Starting anywhere but world 1, level 1 counts as cheated: no save points, no high-score entry. |
| Widescreen | on | Shows the world wider than 4:3 and follows the window up to 2:1. The key and fruit HUD move to the wide corners. Menus, the warning screen and memory-card screens stay 4:3. |
| CD Speed | on, 2x | Shorter loading. 4x is faster but hangs world changes that start past level 1, so the project default is 2x. |

## Requirements

- Your own copy of the game: Kula World PAL, SCES-01000, as `disc/SCES01000.BIN` + `disc/SCES01000.CUE`
  (single data track, MD5 `0f675dc230354f8c3b835bf34841bd20`).
- Optional: a SCPH-1001 BIOS dump as `bios/SCPH1001.BIN`. Without it the bundled OpenBIOS is used.
- [go-task](https://taskfile.dev), CMake, Ninja, a C/C++ compiler, SDL3, Python 3.11+.
  - Alpine: `apk add cmake samurai pkgconf sdl3-dev mesa-dev linux-headers libucontext-dev`
  - macOS: see [docs/BUILD_MACOS.md](docs/BUILD_MACOS.md)

## Build

```sh
git clone --recursive https://github.com/zap0xfce2/kula-world-recompiled.git
cd kula-world-recompiled
# put your disc (and optionally the BIOS) in place, then:
task all        # emitters, generate, dev build with debug server
task build      # release build
task run        # start with the launcher
```

Until [psxrecomp#676](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/psxrecomp/pull/676)
is merged, the `psxrecomp` submodule points at a fork that carries it.

`task --list` shows everything else (tests, lint, smoke test, the psx-beetle
oracle, a level-timer freeze for long test sessions). On macOS pass
`PYTHON=python3.12`. The first generate takes a few minutes; the recompiled C
in `generated/` is not committed.

## Roadmap

Done:
- [x] Disc and EXE analysis; the EXE runs from KUSEG, which upstream had never tested
- [x] Recompilation boots BIOS → title → menu → 3D level, with 0 dispatch misses
- [x] A/B against psx-beetle: identical attract demo and timer values
- [x] macOS build verified (50 fps, audio, memory card, launcher)
- [x] OpenBIOS: plays without a retail BIOS, including memory card saves
- [x] Level Select mod
- [x] Widescreen mod up to 2:1, HUD in the corners, edge culling widened on both sides
- [x] CD Speed default (2x)
- [x] Upstream reports: KUSEG result and portability findings for musl/macOS
- [x] Upstream PR: widescreen band form for register compares ([psxrecomp#676](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/psxrecomp/pull/676))

Next:
- [ ] Widescreen: sky refresh after resizing the window inside a level
- [ ] Widescreen wider than 2:1 (needs a wider generated sky)
- [ ] 60 fps (parked: psxrecomp's frame generation does not see Kula's flips yet; an NTSC-style patch would change the gameplay timing)
- [ ] Own loading screen instead of the piracy warning shown during the first load
- [ ] HD textures, wobble fix
- [ ] Controller test on macOS, ending FMV check
- [ ] Windows build
- [ ] Release packaging

## Known issues

- Widening the window inside a level leaves a gap in the sky until the camera turns.
- Particles can disappear early at the left edge of the widescreen band.
- CD Speed 4x hangs world changes that start past level 1 (cause unknown, 2x is safe).

## Legal

You must own the original game. This repository contains no game data: no
disc image, no BIOS, no extracted assets, no disassembly with original bytes,
and no recompiled game C. Addresses and symbol names used by the mods are
facts about the executable.

Kula World is © 1998 Sony Computer Entertainment Europe, developed by Game
Design Sweden AB. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony.

## Credits

- [psxrecomp](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/psxrecomp) and [recomp-ui](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/recomp-ui): the recompiler, runtime and launcher
- [OpenBIOS](https://github.com/grumpycoders/pcsx-redux) (MIT), bundled with psxrecomp
- [dezgeg/kula-world-decomp](https://github.com/dezgeg/kula-world-decomp): function boundaries, names and addresses used as reference
- The Kula World community documentation at [wiki.kula.quest](https://wiki.kula.quest/)

readme_text:
# Super Dodgeball Recomp **Super Dodge Ball** (NES, 1989, Technōs Japan) recompiled to native C and running on your PC. Not an emulator. The cartridge's 6502 machine code is translated to C at build time and executed natively against a cycle-accurate model of the console. It boots, it plays, and its memory state is byte-for-byte identical to an accurate emulator's from power-on through team select. You bring the ROM. Nothing from the cartridge ships here. ![Super Dodge Ball title screen, recompiled build](docs/assets/title.png) | | | |---|---| | **Playable** | title, menus, team select, and full matches end to end — throws land, damage numbers show, HUD and menus render | | **Verified against** | MesenCE 2.2.1 — 400 frames of RAM, OAM, palette and CIRAM byte-exact from boot · blargg CPU suite 25/25 | | **Mods** | 3, all **off by default** — flicker removal, widescreen with margin sprites, PPU overclocking | | **Engine patches** | 2, both strictly additive and on their way upstream | | **Open bugs** | 2, both in the flicker mod's presentation layer | Built with [NESRecomp](https://github.com/mstan/nesrecomp) by Matthew Stanley — framework questions belong upstream, game-specific issues belong [here](https://github.com/saftle/Super-Dodgeball-Recomp/issues). **This port is in active development; expect rough edges.** > **Fan project.** Unaffiliated with and not endorsed by any rights holder — see > [Legal and project notices](#legal-and-project-notices). No game content is > included; you supply your own legally obtained ROM. Built with substantial AI > assistance — see the [AI disclosure](#ai-disclosure). --- # Playing ## Quick start ```bash # 1. Drop your legally obtained ROM here: # roms/Super Dodge Ball (USA).nes # CRC32 689971F9 · SHA-1 42f954e9bd3256c011aba14c7e5b400abe35fde3 # 2. One-time setup: submodules, engine, patches, MesenCE, first build ./setup.sh # 3. Build and play ./build_and_run.sh ``` The window opens on the launcher — a settings dashboard from [recomp-ui](https://github.com/RetroPortingToolKit/recomp-ui) where you set display, audio and per-player bindings before the game starts. Press **Play**, or **Escape** to skip straight in. Once the game is running, **Escape** opens the in-game menu (display, audio, save states, quit). `setup.sh` needs a C++ compiler, `make`, SDL2 development headers and `xvfb-run`. It prints exactly what is missing and stops rather than failing later.
Just here to play, or curious how it works? Pick your route. - **Just playing** — you are done. `./build_and_run.sh`, then the [Mods screen](#what-this-recomp-adds). - **Building on it** — [Repository layout](#repository-layout) · [the three files that matter](#the-three-files-that-matter) · [headless and scripted runs](#headless-and-scripted-runs) · [verification](#verification) · **[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md)**, which is the operating manual for coding agents on this repo. - **Curious how a recomp works** — [This is a recompiler, not an emulator](#this-is-a-recompiler-not-an-emulator). - **Ambitious** — [Notes from the trenches](#notes-from-the-trenches), which is where most of the interesting mistakes are recorded.
## What this recomp adds Three mods, all in the launcher's **Mods** screen, all **off by default**. With all three off the build is byte-identical to the unmodded game. They are ordinary mod packages — manifests in `mods/packages/`, selectable and deselectable at runtime. Nothing is patched into your ROM, and each section below says exactly what it costs the guest: **widescreen does not touch the guest at all**, the flicker mod makes it emit sprites it had dropped (which shifts its cycle count by a hair without changing how the game plays), and overclocking deliberately changes console timing. ### Remove character flicker *Mods screen → Display* Super Dodge Ball is notorious for flickering characters, and the usual fix does not apply to it. Every emulator's "remove sprite limit" targets the PPU's 8-sprites-per-scanline hardware limit. This game never gets that far — it throttles its own sprites, three separate ways, and in the worst of them the missing tiles are never computed at all. 1. **Half a character.** OAM has 64 slots and a character takes 8, so a full match overflows. The sprite builder hits a hard budget and *stops emitting* — 79% of match frames have someone missing their lower body. This keeps emission going and draws every sprite the game produces. 2. **A whole character, gone 4 frames in 9.** The game builds a display list each frame and deliberately leaves one object off it, rotating which object. Three separate gates on that decision are overridden. 3. **The numbers.** The floating damage digits and the team-select position digits come from two sprite emitters shaped differently enough that nothing had ever captured them — so the one thing on screen that tells you a hit landed was missing entirely. Measured on a match, counting non-background pixels inside a character's box: | | before | after | |---|---|---| | body ink in the truncated character's region, frames 440–469 | stdev **8.7** (flickering) | **0.8** — and **0.0** for the character itself | | culled character's box, frames 700–909 | ink 543–741, stdev **55.0**, missing on 106 of 210 frames | ink 677–741, stdev **16.6**, **0** frames still culled | | damage numbers, frames 895–1400 | never captured | **108 / 108** frames steady | **What it costs.** Game logic is untouched: nothing in the game reads sprite OAM back, and sprite slot 0 never differs on any of 910 measured frames. The truncation half is presentation only — identical cycle count, two bytes of the OAM shadow page differ. The culling half is *not*, and the honest wording is that making the game emit an object it had dropped is extra work the guest then has to do, so its cycle count and NMI phasing shift by a couple of frames and OAM differs on 484 of 910 frames. Nothing in the game can observe any of it — but "cannot observe" is not "byte-identical", and the picture (CIRAM) is identical on 899 of 910. > **Known issue, and the reason this is off by default:** with the mod on, the > level-switch screen after winning a match briefly shows white ghost sprites. Four > candidate fixes were built and measured; each one fixed this and broke something > worse. It needs a signal that the screen changed, and the mod has no notion of a > screen. Details in [`docs/plan.md` 16](docs/plan.md). ### Widescreen *Mods screen → Display* **16:9 / 21:9 / 32:9 — 426 / 560 / 854 columns**, or fit the window. The extra columns show real court, and **the players the NES could not display**. Not upscaled: the same chunky pixels on a wider canvas. This is deliberately *not* wideNES. wideNES warps a framebuffer the NES has already produced, so it can only ever show you what the machine already put on screen — and it ignores sprites entirely, which its own maintainer names as the reason it never shipped. This game's world is different: it is entirely resident in the PPU's nametable before the frame starts (measured byte-identical from frame 450 to frame 900), so a margin pixel can be *read* out of guest state — scroll, world column, tile, attribute, pattern byte, palette — exactly the way the PPU resolves it. **And the sprites are there too.** Super Dodge Ball places every sprite in a 16-bit screen coordinate, computes the tile, the flips, the palette and both halves of the position — and then discards it by truncating one byte, because it lives in a 256-column viewport. Measured over 61 match frames, **40% of the objects on the pitch are off-screen at any moment**. Widescreen recovers that placement and draws it in the margin, facing, animation frame and palette intact. That is the capability wideNES names as the reason it never shipped, and it works here because the guest still knows where the object is. Two options: | Option | Values | | |---|---|---| | **Aspect ratio** | `fit` *(default)* · `16:9` · `21:9` · `32:9` · `stock` | `fit` follows your window's shape. Choose an explicit ratio if you want the width to be independent of the window. | | **Camera** | `follow` *(default)* · `locked` | See below. | Turning it on also reveals the **8 blank columns at the left that the game hides with PPUMASK** — blank in every one of 2112 measured frames. That is not a second toggle. The same compositor draws the court, the margins and those columns, and the combination a separate toggle would permit — widescreen on, reveal off — is a wide frame with a black band at its edge, which is precisely the artefact the feature exists to remove. `SDB_OVERSCAN=0` in the environment forces it back for measurement only. **Camera: `locked`.** The reason is arithmetic rather than taste. The court — everything the machine can ever display — is world columns **40 to 480**, because the game clamps its camera to `[40, 224]` behind a 256-column viewport. That is a **440-column court**, and play never takes the camera outside 102–180. So at 21:9 and 32:9 the **entire court is already on screen at every camera position you will ever reach it from**. The panning adds motion and no information, and it competes with the one thing you are tracking. `locked` pins the canvas to the court and lets the game pan behind it. (16:9 is 426 columns and cannot hold the whole court, so locked centres it and loses 7 columns at each end rather than whichever end the ball happens to be near.) Two details you will notice, both deliberate: - **The HUD stays put.** This game splits its scroll mid-frame — rows 0–47 hold still for the skyline, the player names and the health bars — so the anchor offset is decided *per row*. Anchoring the whole canvas on the court would slide the HUD 6–7 px on every camera step. - **Menus and title screens stay centred.** They are drawn at screen-space columns with a scroll of 0, so the court's window does not describe them and the anchor stands down. The game's own camera clamp is the test, and it is free. The guest is untouched either way: `$C3/$C4`, OAM and the machine's own 256 columns are identical, and `follow` is byte-identical to a build without the setting. **The honest limit.** Past the court's own bounds the margin is the backdrop colour, so at 21:9 and 32:9 there can be a band at either end. That is deliberate. Mirroring and wrapping were both implemented and both rejected on the output: the world's outer band holds the scoreboard and the Statue of Liberty skyline, so mirroring renders the text backwards. **What it costs: nothing.** Presentation only, and proven rather than asserted — a `--frame-log` with the feature on is byte-identical to the same run with it off, on every vector tested (1,200 frames on three of them, 1,500 on the fourth, with and without the reveal): CPU RAM, CIRAM, palette, OAM and the entire 256×240 picture, at an unchanged cycle count. The stock 256 columns in the centre of a wide frame differ from the unmodded game by **zero pixels**. The reconstruction is checked against the machine's own background capture every frame and agrees to 1–2 px out of 61,440; a frame that fails falls back to the ordinary centred picture, which is why title screens and menus just work. Eleven placement and boundary bugs were found and fixed while auditing the margins, **ten of them only by playing the game** and replaying the session. If something looks wrong near an edge, [recording a playthrough](#recording-a-playthrough) is the fastest route to a frame number. ### PPU overclocking *Mods screen → Emulation* Super Dodge Ball feels slower than it should, and the reason is structural: its main loop is an **NMI-synced spin**. It parks waiting for the next NMI, so the 6502 only gets 262 scanlines of CPU per frame. Add **blank scanlines before the NMI** and the guest completes more of its own work before parking again — the game runs faster. Nothing new is drawn. The added lines are blank (rendering is off above scanline 239) and audio pauses across them, so the picture stays 256×240 and the effect is purely extra CPU time. Same mechanism as MesenCE's *Additional scanlines before NMI* and FCEUX's post-render scanlines. Measured against MesenCE at **+12 work-ticks per frame on average, and the lead grows**; on our own backend, 262 lines roughly doubles the per-frame CPU budget and the guest has a populated display list on 565 of 800 frames instead of 316. The Mods screen exposes the count as a slider, **0 to 262**. > **This deliberately changes console timing, so it is off by default and is not > hardware-accurate.** Leave it off if you want original behaviour. ### VSync *Launcher → Graphics → VSync* A toggle in the launcher's Graphics section. With it on, each present syncs to your display's refresh, so motion lands evenly at 60 Hz, 120 Hz or anything else. **Presentation only** — the guest keeps its stock clock either way. Needs `patches/007`, which `setup.sh` applies. Super Dodge Ball is already 60 Hz; there is no 30→60 cap to lift. What this fixes is presentation jitter — every frame used to be presented on a host timer with a few milliseconds of wobble. It cannot subdivide a scroll step the guest never drew, and this game scrolls coarsely: 6–7 pixels in a single frame, never anything between. ## Controls | NES button | Keyboard | Gamepad 1 | |---|---|---| | A | Z | a | | B | X | x | | Select | `\` | back | | Start | Return | start | | Up / Down / Left / Right | Arrow keys | d-pad | | Key | | |---|---| | **Escape** | launcher before boot · in-game menu during play | | **Tab** | fast-forward | | **F8 / F9** | save state · load state | | **F11 / F12** | fullscreen · screenshot | All of these are rebindable in the launcher and persist to `build-cycle/config.ini` beside the executable — delete that file to restore defaults. Player 1 defaults to the keyboard and player 2 to the controller. To build the window without the launcher and in-game menu at all: ```bash NESRECOMP_RECOMP_UI=OFF ./build_and_run.sh ``` ## What is and is not finished **Works:** boot, title, every menu, team select (400 verified frames reach `CHANGE POSITION?` with rosters and courts rendering), and full matches played end to end by scripted runs — throws land, damage digits show, HUD and menus render, an 8000-frame stress run holds. Verification is byte-exact against MesenCE from boot through team select, and blargg's CPU suite passes 25/25 on this engine. **Not tested:** a full playthrough to completion, with a human, including winning rounds and the level-switch screens. That is the main reason the flicker mod stays opt-in. ### Two open bugs - **Bean Ball: the sprite list shrinks while you run the length of the map.** In that game mode — which lets you run across the *entire* map rather than a half-width court — running from one end of the screen to the other makes the flicker mod's presented sprite list decay frame by frame, **53 sprites down to 10**, until a single player sprite remains, cut in half. The background stays perfect (`1183 composed, 1 pillarboxed, seam diff 2 px`) so the compositor is not involved, and the overflow and backstop counters both read 0, so it is not the runaway-list bug. **Not established whether the game emits fewer sprites in that mode or the mod drops them**, and the two need opposite fixes. Full write-up, the frame-by-frame measurements and the next step are in [`docs/plan.md` 14](docs/plan.md). - **A one-frame ghost of a menu character.** A menu screen's character is retired with `y=$F0`, the game then emits nothing for about 14 frames, and the mod repaints it — a jumble of body parts on one frame of a screen transition, flicker mod only. Four rules were built and measured; the nearest miss fixed the ghost cleanly and cost 11% of sweep frames (8 players becoming 4). It needs to know *the screen changed*, and it cannot currently. [`docs/plan.md` 16](docs/plan.md). ### Resolved, and worth not re-investigating - ~~**Sprite judder while the camera pans**~~ — **it is the game's own cadence.** The game updates its camera and its sprite OAM two frames apart, so a running player detaches from the floor for two frames and snaps back. MesenCE reproduces it exactly — same two-frame offset, same base position, same blip — so nothing here is broken and a mod cannot reach it. `python3 tools/tas/judder.py RUN` re-derives the whole thing in one command. - ~~**Widescreen cannot show more world than the game has**~~ — the bound is the game's **camera window**, columns 40 to 480, not the end of the address space. And with `camera = locked` there is no sliding at all. - ~~**Widescreen margins are background only**~~ — part of the feature now, not a toggle. A margin with no players in it is not a wider game. - ~~**Sprites double when both display mods are on**~~ — fixed, with the invariant checked rather than assumed. - ~~**Character flickering**~~ — fixed, all three causes. --- # How it works ## This is a recompiler, not an emulator The cartridge's 6502 machine code is translated to C at build time — one labelled block per ROM instruction, with every CPU cycle's bus activity written out — then compiled to native code and run against a cycle-accurate model of the NES: 6502, PPU, APU, DMAs and the MMC1 mapper. There is no interpreter in the hot path and nothing is decoded at runtime. Two consequences shape everything else in this repo: **The picture is the machine's, not a reconstruction.** The verification that matters is state comparison against an accurate emulator, byte for byte, per video frame — not screenshots that happen to look similar. **The game's own behaviour is available to be read.** RAM the guest wrote is the guest's, and every mod here is built by hooking the game at its own decisions rather than by watching pixels go by. That is also why widescreen can draw a sprite the NES hid: the placement was computed, and only the truncation was thrown away. The cost is that recompilation is one-way. The toolchain goes ROM → C and there is no C → ROM path. Which is also why the repository contains **no ROM and no assets extracted from one** — addresses, sizes and hashes are facts about a cartridge and are fine; bulk game bytes are not, so every hook site is keyed by CRC32 rather than by content. ## Repository layout | Path | | |---|---| | [`src/game.toml`](src/game.toml) | Recompiler config — window title, discovery roots, and twelve content-keyed hook sites | | [`src/sdb_host_extras.c`](src/sdb_host_extras.c) | **All three mods.** The only game-specific C in the tree | | [`src/cycle_seeds.txt`](src/cycle_seeds.txt) | Discovery roots that make the hooked sprite emitters recompiled rather than interpreted | | `mods/packages/` | One manifest-only package per mod, copied beside the executable at build time | | [`CMakeLists.txt`](CMakeLists.txt) | The game project. Sites are keyed by `length` + `crc32` and never by `bytes`, so no ROM data is committed. They declare no `id` — they bind to plugins by address. The subtle part: **a hook site only exists in recompiled code.** Five of the addresses the mods need sit in routines that static discovery never reaches, so they ran on the interpreter — where a hook compiles, binds, and never fires. That is what `src/cycle_seeds.txt` is for: six roots that make them native, at an unchanged total cycle count. A hook declared at an address that discovery never reached looks completely healthy and does nothing. **`src/sdb_host_extras.c`** is the whole of the game-specific work: the flicker mod's sprite capture, host-side redraw and culling override; the overclocking mod, which is just a value handed to the engine's existing extra-scanlines setting; and the widescreen compositor with its margin-sprite capture. One file, three features. **`mods/packages/*/*/manifest.toml`** are declarations, not code. A `.nesmod` archive may not carry native code, so each package is a manifest naming features whose implementation is statically linked into `nes_game` and selected by a stable id. That is also why a package cannot carry a different licence from the code it points at — see [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md). ## Headless and scripted runs ```bash ./build-cycle/nes_game "roms/Super Dodge Ball (USA).nes" [flags] ``` | Flag | | |---|---| | `--frames N` `--input FILE` `--screenshot PATH` | imply headless; `--input` takes an absolute-state schedule (` NAMES`) | | `--ram-init zeros` | **pass this on every comparison run.** Pattern RAM otherwise, and two runs are not comparable | | `--mods-root build-cycle/mods` | the mod catalog. Without it a headless run is stock and stays that way — which is the intended way to A/B a mod | | `--remove-character-flicker` `--ppu-overclock N` `--widescreen MODE` `--margin-sprites 0` | the features, from the command line | | `--present-out PATH --present-every N` | writes what the **window** would show | | `--shot-every N --screenshot PATH` | the machine's native frame | | `--frame-log-at mesen --frame-log FILE` | per-frame state snapshots (RAM, CIRAM, palette, OAM, picture indices) | | `--mem-frame N --mem-out FILE` `--miss-log FILE` `--align 0-3` | memory dump, interpreter-miss log, snapshot alignment | Two of those deserve emphasis, and both have cost real time: **`--present-out` is the only path that exercises a mod.** It writes what the window would show. `--screenshot` and `--frame-log` capture the machine's native 256×240 frame and cannot see any of them. If you are measuring a presentation mod with `--screenshot`, you are measuring nothing. **`--present-every N` is a present interval, not a screenshot density knob.** The compositor only runs when something presents the picture, so `N > 1` skips it — silently, with no warning — and every `drawn` and `composed` figure in this repo is a stride-1 figure. A figure taken at another stride is not a regression, it is meaningless. Measure at 1. A worked example: both display mods on, 900 frames, every frame presented, with the trace that turns "the screen looked wrong somewhere" into a frame number. ```bash SDB_TRACE=1 ./build-cycle/nes_game ROM --frames 900 \ --input tas/vectors/sdb_throw.input --ram-init zeros \ --mods-root build-cycle/mods --remove-character-flicker --widescreen 32:9 \ --present-out tmp/wide/on_%05d.png --present-every 1 ``` One headless gotcha: the widescreen feature's default aspect is `fit`, and `fit` resolves to the **stock 256 columns** when there is no window to follow — so the engine never calls the compositor and the feature appears to do nothing at all. Pass an explicit `--widescreen 16:9` on the command line. ## Verification Three layers, all comparing state rather than pixels. ### Co-simulation against MesenCE One input schedule drives both the cycle backend and an accurate emulator. CPU RAM, CIRAM, palette indices and OAM are diffed byte-exact per video frame, landing on the first divergence. ```bash python3 tools/tas/bk2_to_tas.py tas/vectors/sdb_4976.bk2 tas/sdb_4976.tas.json python3 tools/tas/run_tas.py --tas tas/sdb_4976.tas.json --frames 400 --out tas/runs/r400 python3 tools/tas/diff_tas.py tas/runs/r400 ``` 400 frames reach team select with every byte matching. Sprite palette entry-0 mirrors (`$3F10/$3F14/$3F18/$3F1C`) are masked — hardware mirrors them to the backdrop and the engine's model does not; rendering is unaffected. The TAS is an input source more than an oracle. Super Dodge Ball is a random game, so RNG divergence between the two sides eventually puts them on different paths and a red diff may be that rather than a defect. Investigate the first divergent frame; do not assume a regression. **Ask before running it** — it is minutes of compute, and blargg is upstream's gate rather than this project's. ### blargg's CPU test suite Run against this engine: **25/25** — 20 RAM-text PASS (including `12-jmp_jsr` at 99.4% native, the JSR/RTS case a less careful runtime fails) plus 5 screen-confirmed PASS (`branch_1/2/3`, `dummy_reads`, `timing_test6`). That is a statement about the engine, not about Super Dodge Ball. ```bash python3 tools/blargg/run_blargg.py --tier cpu # ask first — many minutes ``` ### The mods' own gates Each mod has a numbered gate list in [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md), each gate naming the measurement that decides it — margin sprites off vs on must be byte-identical over 700 frames, the machine's own 256 columns must differ by zero pixels, `drawn` and `off-edge` are pinned at 33,885 and 3,951 on the sweep vector. Read those before changing a mod; they encode what is easy to break silently. ### Frame comparison Pixel comparison against MesenCE references is **informational only**. Cross-renderer RGB never matches, because palette emulation differs. State bytes decide; images are for eyeballing. ```bash # 1. Reference frames from MesenCE ./tools/frame_gen/run_frames.sh "roms/Super Dodge Ball (USA).nes" 100 nes_reference --start # 2. The same frames from the cycle backend ./build_and_run.sh --frames 100 --shot-every 1 --screenshot cyc_shots/shot.png # 3. Rename — the backend writes shot_00000.png, MesenCE writes frame_0000.png python3 -c "import glob,os; [os.rename(p,'cyc_shots/frame_%04d.png'%int(p.split('_')[-1].split('.')[0])) for p in glob.glob('cyc_shots/shot_*.png')]" # 4. Compare (tolerance-based: exact RGB never matches across renderers) python3 tools/compare_frames.py --ref nes_reference --recomp cyc_shots --frames 100 ``` Step 3 is not optional — the two renderers use different filename schemes and the comparison silently reads zero frames without it. ### Deeper oracle work For PPU dumps and per-NMI flag logs, `tools/frame_gen/oracle_dump.lua` drives MesenCE directly in `--testRunner` mode: ```bash OUT_DIR=oracle_out DUMP_FRAME=11 MAX_FRAMES=13 HOME="$HOME/mesen-home" \ xvfb-run -a external/mesence/Mesen \ --testrunner "roms/Super Dodge Ball (USA).nes" \ tools/frame_gen/oracle_dump.lua --timeout=60 ``` The isolated `HOME` needs a `settings.json` (`AllowIoOsAccess`, `ScriptTimeout: 60`, `RamPowerOnState: 1`). Note the trap recorded in [Notes from the trenches](#prove-the-harness-can-see-the-effect-first) — MesenCE reads that file from beside its own executable, not from `$HOME`. ## Recording a playthrough Because sometimes the gate you need is a human holding a controller. Hand-written vectors fail here for reasons nobody could read off the code: the game's input window opens at frame 594 and *silently drops* direction presses aimed before it, and one whole class of margin bug only appears once a character has walked clean across the edge rather than stepped over it once. **Ten of the eleven margin bugs were found this way and by no other means.** ```bash tools/play_record.sh bar-artifact 2000 ``` Plays in a window and leaves a replayable `--input` vector, an `SDB_TRACE=1` log and a screenshot per frame in `tmp/bar-artifact/`. Close the window when you have what you came for — the vector records the true frame count, but only if you close it rather than killing it. | | | |---|---| | `SDB_MODS` | which mods are on, from `remove-character-flicker`, `widescreen`, `ppu-overclock`. Default `remove-character-flicker,widescreen` | | `SDB_ASPECT` | `16:9` *(default)* · `21:9` · `32:9` · `stock`. Note this script defaults to 16:9 even though the **launcher** defaults to `fit` | | `SDB_CAMERA` | `follow` (default) or `locked` | | `SDB_OVERSCAN` | `0` forces the clipped-column reveal off, for the headless A/B | | `SDB_SCANLINES` | overclock scanlines, `0..262`. **Changes guest timing**, so such a capture compares against no stock figure in the docs | | `SDB_SHOT_EVERY` | **present** every N frames, not a screenshot interval | | `SDB_SCALE` · `SDB_FRAMES` · `SDB_UNLIMITED` | window scale · frame cap · run until closed | Two traps worth knowing before you read a capture: - **A replayed vector must be replayed in a window, never headless.** The windowed and headless hosts do not run the same guest state — see [Notes from the trenches](#notes-from-the-trenches). - **Analyse a capture where it was made.** `trace.log` is the ground truth and `tools/widescreen/margin_track.py` reads it directly, needing no replay at all. ## MesenCE, the reference emulator `setup.sh` handles this: it clones MesenCE and builds it, or uses an existing binary. If you add one, that is the tool you measure it with. --- # Notes from the trenches The bug log here is mostly a record of instruments that reported success while measuring nothing, which is the failure mode AI-assisted code invites. These are the ones that cost the most time, written down so the next person does not pay them again. ## A green gate that measured nothing Three separate instruments produced **a clean-looking pass over zero examined frames**. A hand-formatted trace line lost a newline and the per-sprite audit's regex matched nothing — it reported "no lines in that log" on exactly the runs where the trace had been switched on to run it. The fix then hit the mirror-image fault and matched zero of 701 lines, still reporting the same reassuring message. A bounds gate formatted its input filenames from an assumed pattern, read zero files, and exited clean. The shape is always the same: **an instrument that cannot fire is indistinguishable from one reporting nothing wrong.** Check that a gate *ran* — it should print a per-object table, not silence — before believing it. The structural fix was to stop parsing a hand-formatted trace at all and emit one JSON object per line, which cannot care where a closer was printed. ## Windowed and headless are not the same game Two windowed runs of one schedule are byte-identical to each other, which is what makes a played session reproducible. **A headless replay of that same recorded vector is not.** Frames 0–3 match; frame 4 diverges (scroll 32 against 256) and the run ends on a different game state — 2,666 against 2,121 off-edge captures, 32,200 against 15,504 margin sprites drawn, 769 against 752 frames composed. Pacing cannot cause it, and it is not the input: the recorded frames are exactly the frames the schedule fired on, and the divergence starts four frames *before* the first press. **Cause is unattributed. Do not guess.** What it does establish is a rule: analyse a windowed capture where it was made, and never validate a windowed feature by replaying it headless. ## Screenshots can slow the game down Capturing with `--present-out` does a full-renderer readback per frame, so the cost scales with the window's pixel count. At `WindowScale = 3` fullscreen it measures **41 fps instead of 60**, and at 720p capturing every frame, **29 fps** — and because audio is generated per emulated frame, **the game goes into slow motion with the sound**, which is very hard to mistake for a performance bug. It is not vsync (identical either way) and it is not the PNG encode (compressing first barely helps — the readback dominates). Pin the capture resolution to `WindowScale = 1` and the problem disappears. It is a correctness non-issue: the guest state is identical, and two runs are comparable on state — but wall clock and audio are both wrong, which makes the run unplayable and the timings meaningless. ## 386 "content mismatches" that were the point Hook sites report ~386 content mismatches and the flicker sites report zero. That is the mechanism working, not a defect. MMC1 maps a different 16 KB bank at the same address at different times, and the hook layer tests the address *bit* alone before checking the bytes in the currently mapped bank. The declared CRC is confirmed correct by the fact that 4,150 callbacks fire — a wrong key could never fire at all — and the rejections are the other banks, with the guest byte-identical throughout. **Do not "fix" this by changing the CRC.** A mismatched site is the content key doing its job. ## The wrong question, asked three times The recurring mistake in this repository is asking live OAM whether the machine currently holds a given sprite. Three separate fixes were built on that question — a ghost filter in the overscan band, a band anchor, and a basis choice — and all three acted on the answer "the machine did not emit it this frame". That is **exactly the truncation the flicker mod exists to undo**, and the PPU could not have painted those columns anyway, so every skip left a hole that nothing else filled. Two of the three were introduced *as* fixes for artifacts they could not explain, and one of them suppressed 129 legitimate parts and was then credited with fixing 129 others. The rule that came out of it: **match on world column, vote with at least two parts, and never let a missing sprite become a reason to draw less.** ## The art is not a fact about the limits Widescreen's margin originally ended where the *nametable art* suggested the world ended — by measuring how many tiles in from the edge repeated that edge column. That was right on the stadium by luck, because its end wall happens to be a uniform band. On the London course, whose edge column varies immediately, it collapsed to a one-tile floor and produced **no bound at all** — drawing past the court's own edge for a whole 4,355-frame played session, and only being caught because the backdrop there is a dark blue rather than black, so a scan for "not black" reports a full backdrop as content. The bound was in the game's code the whole time: two immediate operands at the camera clamp, giving world columns 40 to 480. No per-level table, no measurement, and both ends of the evidence agreed with the disassembly rather than being fitted to it. **The art of an end wall is not a fact about the game's limits; the camera is.** ## Prove the harness can see the effect first The first PPU-overclocking measurement concluded that overclocking changed nothing. It had changed nothing because the setting had never reached the emulator — the sandbox put `settings.json` in `$HOME`, and MesenCE reads it from beside its own executable. The control that caught it was wall clock: a setting that quadruples PPU work *must* change how long a run takes, and 0.606 s against 0.612 s says it didn't. The same class of bug hit the mod itself — the engine zeroes the extra-scanlines field *after* mods activate, so the feature reported itself active while running stock timing. **A negative result from a tool never tested against a known positive is not a negative result.** Ask what result would prove the instrument works, then go and get it. ## Play it Ten of the eleven margin-sprite bugs were found by recording and replaying a played session. They survived the sweep vector, the pan vector, the idle vector and an 8,000-frame throw stress run, because every one of them needs a state a script cannot be talked into — the court input window opens at frame 594, a boundary artifact needs the camera to pan the whole width, one bug needs the player to actually run. The eleventh was **not**, and it is the instructive one: a duplicated sprite at the seam that flickered while the camera panned sat on a committed vector the whole time, because the audit in use compares the margin against *itself* and cannot see a margin that is internally consistent and a whole camera step away from the machine. Worth knowing before you reach for the gamepad again — and worth knowing before you trust a green audit. ## Rules that are not negotiable - **Never commit ROM-derived bytes.** No tile, CHR, nametable, attribute or palette arrays, no `.db` dumps, no multi-line disassembly excerpts. Addresses, sizes and hashes are facts and are fine. Hook sites are keyed by `crc32` for exactly this reason. - **Ask before installing packages, deleting the venv, or committing.** - **One `nes_game` per mods directory.** `build-cycle/mods/state.toml` is shared mutable state; two concurrent runs can leave the feature disabled and the whole run silently go native. - **A `state.toml` naming a feature this build does not have hard-fails the whole catalog**, rather than degrading to stock. Delete it and let the launcher rewrite it. - **Never edit `generated/`.** Fix the recompiler or `game.toml`. - **Pin the submodules.** The launcher's C ABI is append-only and heavily churned; headers and sources must come from one revision. - Every third-party addition ships with provenance and a licence posture recorded at add time, in [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md) or the nearest README — never as later cleanup. --- # ROM, references and notices ## ROM specifications No ROM ships here and no assets are extracted from one.
